strengths: LPAM addresses a practical stitching problem: residual local misalignment that seam selection alone cannot repair. Its modular design offers a useful way to improve existing pipelines without retraining.

Tables 1–2 report consistent improvements across four seam-cutting methods, five upstream alignment methods, and 79 image pairs from three datasets. For example, baseline seam SSIM on SEAGULL increases from 0.638 to 0.697.
Figures 1, 5, and 7 show visible improvements in structural continuity. Combining localized dense alignment with flow modulation and constrained seam reconnection is a sensible engineering approach.

The pipeline and pseudocode are understandable, established components and datasets are cited, and a code URL is provided. The parameter ablations and candid discussion of failures with small patches strengthen the presentation.
weaknesses: The quantitative evaluation does not adequately establish overall mosaic quality. Equations (6–9) measure agreement between image patches around the seam and can miss deformation or discontinuities elsewhere. Table 3 exposes this problem: removing sigmoid modulation improves SEAGULL SSIM from 0.697 to 0.768, although the manuscript explains that this can introduce boundary artifacts. Independent perceptual or structural evaluation is needed to validate the central alignment-versus-boundary-consistency tradeoff.

The originality and comparative advantage are insufficiently established relative to prior seam-guided alignment. Section 2 already describes adaptive alignment in SEAGULL [22] and dense-flow-based seam/warp estimation in [35], making the subsequent characterization of prior methods as operating on settled prealigned images too broad. Figure 7 provides a qualitative comparison with [22,31], but quantitative quality and runtime comparisons with closely related refinement approaches are missing.

The seam acceptance rule in Section 3.2 has a concrete weakness: max(Q) <= 1.5 mean(Q) accepts a uniformly high-error seam as plausible. It measures relative variation rather than absolute alignment quality and can therefore skip repair when misalignment is widespread. No threshold sensitivity or detection analysis establishes how often this matters, weakening the claim that seam quality is dissociated from initial alignment accuracy.

Important implementation details remain underspecified in the supplied manuscript, including padding of repair rectangles, handling of overlapping patches, modulation direction beyond the horizontal example, SIFT-flow settings, and image resolutions. Patch extent directly affects the documented failure case, so these details matter for reproducing both quality and timing results.

The efficiency claim needs stronger context. Section 4.4 reports roughly 6–10 seconds for LPAM alone, while several host seam-cutting methods take approximately 3.5–9.6 seconds, excluding initial alignment. This is substantial additional computation. Without total-runtime comparisons against competing refinement methods or evidence of scaling with image and patch size, the claimed lightweight advantage remains uncertain.

All four quantitative metrics measure agreement between image patches along the selected seam; they do not adequately capture distortion or discontinuities introduced elsewhere. Table 3 exposes this limitation: removing sigmoid attenuation improves most reported metrics despite producing boundary artifacts. Independent assessment of complete mosaics, such as blinded preferences or structural-artifact counts, together with per-pair improvement and failure rates, is needed.

The distinctive contribution is targeted postprocessing, but its novelty and advantage over existing seam-guided alignment remain insufficiently established. SEAGULL [22] already refines alignment using seam information, and [35] combines dense matching with seam estimation and warping. Quantitative quality-versus-cost comparisons and an ablation against simpler dense-refinement alternatives would better establish the contribution.

The seam acceptance criterion in Section 3.2 has a substantive blind spot: uniformly high errors satisfy max(Q) <= 1.5 mean(Q), so a consistently poor seam can be declared plausible and receive no repair. This exposes continued dependence on mostly successful initial alignment, contrary to the broad claim of dissociating seam quality from initial alignment accuracy. Neither sensitivity to k nor the frequency of such failures is evaluated.

The claimed boundary-consistency guarantee does not follow from the formulation. With beta = 8, Equation (5) gives f(0) approximately 0.018 and f(1) approximately 0.982, and its one-dimensional ramp does not impose continuity along every rectangular patch edge. Fixing boundary labels preserves label compatibility but does not itself preserve pixel continuity. The formulation should be presented as a heuristic, with its boundary-artifact tradeoff measured more systematically.

Reproducibility and efficiency evidence remain incomplete. The supplied manuscript does not specify important SIFT-flow settings, precise patch padding and overlap handling, or evaluation image resolutions. Section 4.4 reports roughly 6–10 seconds for LPAM separately from the host seam cutter and excludes initial alignment; this overhead is substantial relative to several hosts. Resolution-dependent scaling and comparable total-pipeline timings are needed to substantiate the efficiency claim.

Originality and comparative advantage are insufficiently established relative to seam-guided local alignment [22] and dense-matching seam estimation [35]. The characterization of prior methods as operating on fixed pre-alignments is too broad given the paper’s own related-work discussion. Parallax and SEAGULL receive only a qualitative comparison in Figure 7, and [35] is not evaluated. Comparisons with existing seam-guided refinement and a simple full-seam-band flow baseline would help isolate the benefit of selective patch repair.

The seam-quality gate has a concrete robustness problem. Section 3.2 accepts a seam whenever max(Q) ≤ 1.5 mean(Q), which also accepts uniformly poor seams—for example, Q = 0.8 everywhere. This tests relative variation rather than absolute quality. Without a safeguard or evaluation across initial-misalignment severity, the claim that LPAM dissociates seam quality from initial alignment is not supported.

Boundary consistency is asserted more strongly than the formulation justifies. The one-dimensional sigmoid in Equation (5) does not reach exactly zero or one at the endpoints and does not establish continuity around the full rectangular boundary. Fixing boundary labels connects seams but does not itself ensure image continuity. Crop padding, overlapping-patch handling, flow settings, and orientation selection also need clearer specification for reproducibility.

The computational-efficiency claim needs qualification. Section 4.4 reports host and LPAM times separately: on SEAGULL, baseline seam cutting takes 4.11 seconds and LPAM adds 7.34 seconds, producing approximately 2.79 times the original seam-stage cost. Image-resolution scaling and matched quality–runtime comparisons are missing, so the efficiency advantage over competing refinement strategies remains unclear.
